name: inline-functions
intent: Collapse a function call into its call site - deliberately where the compiler will not do it, or across a translation-unit boundary where it structurally cannot - so the call overhead, the argument marshalling and the indirection disappear and the arguments become constants the optimiser can fold.
problem: The compiler refuses to inline across a module boundary, refuses anything above its cost budget, and often declines a call it should take because the function is large or the address escapes. What remains is a real call: arguments pushed or moved, a return address, a frame, and an indirect branch that the CPU's predictor must get right. For a function called in a tight loop this is often the dominant cost - not the arithmetic. And a virtual or generic call in another module is the same story with a worse indirection, because the callee is unknown at compile time.
context: Applies when profiling shows call overhead dominating a hot path and the compiler declined to inline: a small function on the critical path, a getter or comparison in a tight loop, a polymorphic or virtual call that devirtualisation could not resolve, a hot function in a library where the call site cannot see its body. Cross-module cases dominate real systems: the Rust standard library's generics are instantiated in the caller's crate (which is why #[inline] on a generic is an optimisation hint, not a style choice), Java's and C#'s JIT inlines aggressively only within a compilation unit unless hot, and C++'s One Definition Rule means the definition must be visible. It does not apply when the cost is memory or I/O rather than call overhead, and manual inlining is usually the wrong answer to a memory problem.
benefits: Removes the call overhead that profiling shows is dominant: the argument shuffling, the frame setup, the return, and the indirect branch - which also removes a branch-predictor entry from the hot loop.

Turns arguments into constants the optimiser can use: an inlined call with a literal argument lets constant folding, dead-code elimination and further inlining cascade, so the win compounds beyond the call itself.
Enables devirtualisation and dynamic dispatch removal: an inline hint on a virtual function lets the compiler see the dynamic type at the call site and replace the virtual call with a direct one.

Removes a cross-module barrier: because a compiler cannot inline a function whose body it has not seen, marking a small cross-crate function for inlining is often the only way to get the win in Rust, Swift, and C++ header-only libraries.
Enables better register allocation: the caller's and callee's live values share registers, so the register pressure of a boundary disappears and the surrounding code optimises better.
It is bounded and local: unlike an algorithmic change, forcing inlining in one function is a contained, measurable, revertable edit with a clear hypothesis.
tradeoffs: Code size grows, and code size is not free: exceeding the instruction-cache (i-cache) or the instruction-decode bandwidth can slow the function down even as it speeds up the call, so a hot loop can get slower when a big body is inlined into it.

Inlining cost is superlinear: inlining a large body into many call sites multiplies its size, increasing compile time, binary size and link time, and the compiler's own budget exists precisely to prevent this.

It exposes register pressure and can hurt: inlining a body with high register pressure into a hot loop can cause spills that the call boundary was actually hiding, so the 'obvious' win becomes a loss.

The compiler was right to decline: a refused inline is usually the compiler's cost model correctly predicting that inlining would not help, and forcing it overrides a decision made with better information.

Manual inlining destroys the abstraction and the ability to change it: the body is duplicated at every call site, so a fix to the function must be applied everywhere, and the code no longer says what it does.

It is not portable and not stable across compilers or versions: the benefit depends on the toolchain's cost model, so the same hint can help on one compiler, do nothing on another, and regress on the next release.
Inlining a function that is never actually hot wastes code size for nothing, and the compiler's inability to know the call site is hot is the whole difficulty - a hint is a guess.
Debugging and profiling get harder: inlined frames do not appear in stack traces, so a crash inside an inlined body reports the caller, and an inlined-into-the-caller loop is harder to attribute.
quality_attributes_note: Performance is high but conditional - it only helps when call overhead was genuinely dominant, and it can lose to code-size effects. Extensibility is the lowest score of any pattern here: inlining duplicates the body, so changing it means changing every copy, which is the direct cost of the decision to stop treating it as one function.

participants.responsibility: The call site that absorbs the body; it gains the constant arguments and loses the abstraction boundary.
participants.notes: Every caller of an inlined function is a maintenance copy of its body.

participants.responsibility: The body to be collapsed into the caller; it must be small and its address must not escape.
participants.notes: Taking its address prevents inlining, because the function must exist as an entity.

participants.responsibility: The declaration that raises the inlining priority or forces the collapse.
participants.notes: In C++ this is also an ODR/linkage rule, not only a hint.

participants.responsibility: Decides whether to inline based on its cost budget; the hint either raises priority or overrides the decision.
participants.notes: A refused inline is usually a correct prediction that it would not help.

participants.responsibility: The visibility barrier that makes inlining impossible without a hint, and the place where the hint matters most.
participants.notes: The compiler cannot inline what it cannot see - this is why the Rust #[inline] on a generic is load-bearing.

participants.responsibility: The finite on-chip cache of instructions; the limit that inlining trades against.
participants.notes: When a loop no longer fits, it fetches instructions from memory and every other optimisation is wasted.

use_cases: Small functions on a measured hot path: a getter, a comparison, a clamp, a bounds check in a tight loop, where the profile shows the call not the body dominating.

Rust generics in a library crate: #[inline] on a generic function is required for the code to be instantiated in the caller's crate, so cross-crate inlining (and the resulting constant propagation) can happen at all.

Swift public functions in a library: @inlinable exposes the body to the client's optimiser, without which cross-module optimisation is impossible - the documentation notes @inlinable is not for most functions.

Java and Kotlin hot virtual methods: the JIT inlines a monomorphic call site and refuses a polymorphic one, so a hot call site's cost is usually a devirtualisation problem and inlining the callee lets the JIT resolve it.

C++ header-only libraries and templates: the body must be visible for instantiation and optimisation, which is the whole reason templates and header-only libraries are faster than shared-library alternatives.
A hot loop whose body was outlined by the optimiser (a loop too large to inline whose overhead was measured), where forcing the inline restores the constant-folded trip count.
A function whose address is taken rarely but which is called in the hottest path - inlining the call site (not the address) removes the overhead where it matters.
Devirtualisation: marking a small virtual function inlinable lets a compiler or JIT replace the indirect call with a direct one at the monomorphic call site, removing a hard-to-predict branch.
avoid_when: The profile shows memory or I/O dominating, not call overhead - inlining a function that then misses cache does nothing for the latency that matters.
The function is large, or has a large body relative to the loop it is in - the code size exceeds the i-cache and the call gets slower, which is exactly what the compiler's budget prevents.
The body has high register pressure - inlining it into a tight loop can cause spills the call boundary was hiding, making things worse.
The compiler already declined for a good reason - its cost model saw more information than the hint provides; forcing it overrides a better-informed decision.
The call is genuinely not hot - the hint wastes code size in every call site for a path that is never taken, and the compiler cannot know which is which.
The function must remain one function - a callback, a virtual override, a function whose address is compared or stored, or anything whose identity is observable cannot be inlined away.
Portability or maintainability matters more than the last few percent - the benefit is compiler-dependent, and duplicating the body across call sites makes every future change a cross-cutting edit.
Debuggability is a requirement - an inlined frame does not appear in a stack trace, so a crash inside the body reports the caller.
pitfalls: Inlining a function whose address is taken: the compiler must emit a real copy, so the hint does nothing and the body is duplicated anyway - the addressable function still exists.

Forcing always_inline on a large or recursive function: a recursive inline never terminates the expansion and the compiler either rejects it or explodes; a large body multiplies code size at every call site.

Devirtualising away a real polymorphic call: marking a virtual function inlinable makes a monomorphic call site faster, but if a second implementation is ever instantiated the call site becomes megamorphic and the JIT's inline cache fails - a performance cliff when the second subclass appears.
Inlining a function with a large stack frame into a loop, causing a stack growth or a prologue in the hot path that the call boundary was amortising.

Overshooting the instruction cache: a hot loop that no longer fits in the i-cache fetches instructions from memory, and every arithmetic optimisation inside it is wasted - measure the instruction footprint, not just the wall time of one run.
Assuming the hint is portable: inlining a std::vector growth path, or an alloc function, can change allocation behaviour under a different standard library, not just speed.

Inlining an out-of-line definition that changes the linkage or the ODR in C++: a function declared inline must be defined identically in every translation unit, so moving a definition into a header to enable inlining is an ODR change as well as a performance one.

Chasing an inlining win into a benchmark that does not represent production - the call is inlined in the benchmark because the compiler can see it, and the production code has the same call but a different budget.

related_patterns_notes.data-locality: The co-equal performance technique, and the one that must be tried first. Inlining removes call overhead; data-locality removes cache misses. When a profile shows memory stalls, layout beats inlining almost every time, and the two together are how a hot loop is made to stream.
related_patterns_notes.prefetching: The other latency technique, complementary rather than alternative: inlining makes the address computation visible so prefetch can be placed, and prefetch hides the miss that inlining cannot remove.
related_patterns_notes.double-buffer: Removes a whole class of synchronisation by overlap rather than by optimising the operation - a structural change that often beats inlining the operations inside the swap, and never duplicates a body across call sites.
related_patterns_notes.macro-method: The pattern of restricting a method's body to named steps for readability; inlining is its performance counterpart - collapsing the steps into one body trades the readability this catalog's macro-method record preserves for call-overhead removal, and the two pull in opposite directions on purpose.
related_patterns_notes.template-method: The OO answer to inlining: templates are instantiated at the call site, so the body is specialised and inlinable by construction - the type-level way to get what an inline keyword gives at the source level.
related_patterns_notes.small-object-optimization: Both avoid a pointer chase or a call by keeping the data local - small-object keeps a value inside its handle so no allocation and no indirection; inlining removes the indirection of a call.
related_patterns_notes.object-pool: The reuse counterpart: pooling avoids constructing and destructing an object on a hot path, which is a different cost (allocation) that inlining does not address.
related_patterns_notes.copy-and-swap: Inlining a copy-and-swap makes the temporary disappear when the copy is cheap, but the pattern's reason for existing is exception safety, not speed - inlining it does not remove the need for the temporary.
related_patterns_notes.strategy: Strategy selects behaviour via a virtual call - the exact call inlining devirtualises. A monomorphic strategy call site is a prime inlining target; a polymorphic one is where the technique fails.
related_patterns_notes.tail-recursion: The other compiler-driven optimisation: a tail call is rewritten to a jump automatically, which is the same elimination of the return address that inlining performs by hand - proof that the compiler already does it when it can see the whole call site, which is precisely when you do not need the hint.
related_patterns_notes.double-dispatch: The pattern that exists specifically to make a call site see two concrete types instead of a polymorphic one. It is the answer to the megamorphic-site problem inlining cannot solve: rather than hoping the compiler devirtualises, the dispatch is arranged so the compiler can see which method runs.
related_patterns_notes.delegation: A delegating wrapper is the manual form of devirtualisation: replacing a virtual call with a direct call to a stored concrete delegate. It is faster and it breaks substitutability, which is the same trade inlining makes and the reason it is reserved for measured hot paths.

anti_patterns: Spraying inline hints across a codebase instead of inlining the one measured hot path - the cost is code size and maintenance, and the benefit is nowhere near the hot path.
Forcing always_inline on a large function, which multiplies its body at every call site and can exceed the i-cache, making the supposedly-faster loop slower.
Using inlining to fix a memory-latency problem: the profile said the loop stalls on cache misses, and inlining the caller does nothing for them.
Manually copying a function body into several call sites to 'avoid the call', duplicating logic that then drifts between the copies and is impossible to change in one place.
Inlining a virtual method to devirtualise a call site that later becomes polymorphic, turning a fast monomorphic site into a megamorphic one that is slower than the original.
Trusting the hint without measuring, so a regression lands on hardware or a compiler where the inliner budget is different.
Inlining in a way that defeats devirtualisation's cache benefit or increases register pressure enough to cause spills in the hot loop.
Assuming a benchmark win transfers to production, where the same code is called through a path the benchmark does not model.
design_principles: Measure before forcing: an inlining decision is a hypothesis about where the time goes, and the profile is the test of that hypothesis.
Let the compiler decide where it can: a hint is only needed where the compiler lacks the information (a cross-module boundary) or the budget is too conservative for a measured hot path.
Trade size for speed deliberately: inlining spends instruction-cache capacity and binary size for call-overhead removal, and the exchange is only worth it when call overhead is measurably dominant.
Keep one copy: prefer a compiler-visible single definition (generics, header-only, @inlinable) over duplicating the body by hand, so the abstraction survives.
Prefer structural fixes: an algorithmic or layout change removes the cost; inlining removes the call, and the call is only the cost when the profile says so.
best_practices: Profile first and confirm the cost is call overhead (instruction counts, branch-misprediction on the call, the cycles attributed to the callee) rather than memory or I/O.
Add #[inline] / inline / @inlinable to small, frequently-crossed-boundary functions (getters, comparisons, generic instantiations, small library helpers), not to large bodies.
Reserve always_inline for the one measured case where the compiler declined a hot path, and re-measure the instruction-cache footprint afterwards.
In Rust, mark generic functions #[inline] so they are instantiated in the calling crate; this is the idiomatic and necessary case, not a micro-optimisation.

In C++, prefer header-only or template instantiation (the body visible at the call site) over the inline keyword on an out-of-line definition, and respect the ODR when moving a definition to a header.
Keep manual inlining out of the codebase entirely - if the body must be duplicated, fix the abstraction (a generic, a macro generating one definition) rather than copying it.
After inlining, re-run the whole benchmark: a megamorphic call site or an i-cache miss can make the 'faster' version slower, and only a full run shows it.
Document why a specific inline hint exists and what measurement justified it, so a future toolchain upgrade knows when to remove it.
Check the target's inliner budget and the debug/release build difference: the optimisation exists only in the release build, so a test in debug mode tells you nothing about the effect.
sources: cppreference.com, 'inline function' - the C++ semantics of inline (multiple definitions permitted, ODR consequences), that it is a hint the compiler is not required to follow, and that it exists for linkage and optimisation rather than as a command. https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/inline

Swift documentation, 'Inlinable' / '@inlinable' - the attribute that exposes a declaration's body for cross-module optimisation, with the explicit guidance that it is not appropriate for most functions and carries a code-size cost. https://docs.swift.org/swift-book/documentation/the-swift-programming-language/attributes/#inlinable

LLVM documentation, 'How to Write a Loop' / inline cost model - the compiler-side view that inlining is a cost-bounded decision (the inline cost model with threshold) rather than a per-function command, which is why a hint raises priority and an always-inline overrides it. https://llvm.org/docs/LoopVectorize.html

Rustonomicon / The Rust Programming Language, 'Generic Code' - why #[inline] on a generic is required for cross-crate inlining and code generation, and the performance note that generic functions should carry the hint. https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch10-01-syntax.html

Wikipedia, 'Inlining' - the general trade-off between call overhead and code size, the instruction-cache limit that bounds inlining, and the history of the heuristic in compilers. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inlining
